item.title: Mainland criticizes Taiwan's 'defense' spending, warns of resource depletion
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-28
Mainland criticizes Taiwan's 'defense' spending, warns of resource depletion Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities' squandering of public resources in pursuit of militarization will ultimately deplete the island, a Chinese defense ministry spokesperson said on Thursday. Commenting on the "defense" budget recently proposed by the Lai Ching-te authorities, Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, said the DPP authorities are acting against the mainstream aspirations of the Taiwanese public for peace and development. According to reports, the island's executive department has proposed a record NT$1.12 trillion ($35.2 billion) "defense" budget for 2027, exceeding NT$1 trillion for the first time. The figure represents an 18.2 percent increase from the 2026 budget. Zhang accused the Lai authorities of going to great lengths to curry favor with external forces, recklessly squandering public resources and pursuing militarization. "This has severely undermined the well-being of people on the island and will ultimately deplete Taiwan's resources, leaving the authorities facing their eventual downfall," Zhang said. He also stressed that the historical trend toward reunification is unstoppable, warning the DPP authorities that no matter how many military exercises they conduct, they cannot change the inevitable demise of "Taiwan independence".

item.title: DPP slammed for ignoring public will
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
DPP slammed for ignoring public will As the Democratic Progressive Party authorities in Taiwan tightened restrictions on cross-Strait exchanges, the Chinese mainland condemned them for going against public opinion and continuing to engage in political manipulation. At a regular news conference on Wednesday, Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, urged the DPP authorities to heed calls from the island's business and industrial communities, promptly remove unreasonable restrictions that obstruct cross-Strait exchanges and facilitate cross-Strait integrated development. On Monday, Taiwan's federation of industries, the island's largest business organization, issued a white paper calling on the DPP authorities to simplify the screening process for mainland professionals traveling to Taiwan. Regarding calls from Taiwan's business and industrial communities for smoother cross-Strait exchanges, Zhang said they reflect the will of the people and the broader trend, adding that the mainland has been taking measures to facilitate travel and exchanges between people on both sides. The tourism sector in Taiwan has also called for greater exchanges with the mainland. The tourism association of Penghu county recently urged Taiwan's "mainland affairs council" to resume the "mini three links" connecting Penghu with mainland coastal cities. The DPP authorities responded that there are currently no plans to resume the links, citing so-called security concerns. The "mini three links" refer to direct passenger, postal and trade links between coastal areas of Fujian province and Jinmen and Matsu, which serve as major channels for personnel exchanges between Fujian and Taiwan. As the mainland has promoted the resumption of travel by residents of Shanghai and Fujian to Jinmen and Matsu, about 350,000 trips have been made by residents of the two mainland regions to Jinmen and Matsu via the passenger routes of the "mini three links" since August 2024, Zhang said. Zhang accused the DPP authorities of disregarding public opinion and engaging in political manipulation, saying their actions have lost public support. "The DPP authorities are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait exchanges," she said. Taiwan's education authorities recently said the "registration platform", which requires schools on the island to submit information when taking part in exchange activities on the mainland, has been further improved. Schools that provide false information could face reductions in future subsidies for exchange activities. "The DPP authorities have resorted to every possible means to disrupt normal educational exchanges and interactions between young people and students on both sides of the Taiwan Strait," Zhang said, adding that the move exposed the authorities' ulterior motive of obstructing personnel exchanges and escalating confrontation and hostility across the Strait. She also criticized the DPP authorities for fabricating data to justify banning mainland social media platforms. Taiwan's "interior affairs department" recently claimed that the number of fraud cases had declined after RedNote, or Xiaohongshu, was banned on the island in December last year, and said the app could face another one-year ban. Describing the DPP's moves as depriving Taiwan people of their right to know and their freedom to use social media platforms, Zhang said such misguided actions cannot dampen Taiwan people's enthusiasm for communicating through mainland social media platforms, nor can they stop the growing public desire on both sides of the Strait to strengthen ties and draw closer to each other.

item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities pose biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges: spokeswoman
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
Taiwan's DPP authorities pose biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges: spokeswoman BEIJING -- Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities have been acting as the biggest barrier to cross-Strait exchanges, a mainland spokeswoman said on Wednesday. Zhang Han, spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, made the remarks at a news conference when asked for comments on the DPP authorities' tight vetting on students applying for education exchange programs on the mainland. "The DPP authorities have gone extreme lengths to obstruct normal education and youth exchanges across the Strait," Zhang said, noting that the move has exposed their malicious agenda of escalating cross-Strait confrontation and antagonism. Peace, development, exchanges and cooperation represent mainstream public opinion in Taiwan, said Zhang. "The desire of compatriots across the Strait for closer ties and the momentum of exchanges and cooperation are unstoppable." While revealing that the DPP authorities are intentionally creating "information cocoon" in Taiwan, Zhang extended an invitation to the people of Taiwan to visit the mainland and see the real mainland for themselves. The spokeswoman also called on people from Taiwan to stay clear-headed in the face of Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te's separatist rhetoric and take a firm stand against "Taiwan independence" separatist acts.

item.title: Comment on Taiwan TV draws criticism on both sides of the Strait
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-27
Comment on Taiwan TV draws criticism on both sides of the Strait A comment made on a Taiwan TV program claiming that "there are no refrigerators in Beijing" has drawn criticism on both sides of the Taiwan Strait. "Such remarks, which are detached from reality, will only make a laughingstock of themselves," Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news conference on Wednesday. She said the Democratic Progressive Party authorities have imposed restrictions on and obstructed cross-Strait exchanges and interactions, deliberately creating an "information cocoon" on the island in an attempt to prevent Taiwan residents from learning about the mainland. "We welcome Taiwan residents to break through these barriers, visit the mainland more often and see for themselves the real and vibrant mainland," Zhang said. On a Taiwan TV program called Newswawawa, Liao Mei-ran, a self-described "fortune teller", claimed that during a visit to the mainland, she found "there were no refrigerators in Beijing, and people in Beijing did not have cold drinks". The remark drew attention on both sides of the Strait. Some Taiwan netizens said it reflected the extent to which the island has become an "information cocoon". "While it may appear that you are mocking the mainland, in fact, it is Taiwan that is embarrassing itself," one commenter wrote.

item.title: Animal communicator heals pet owners' hearts
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
Animal communicator heals pet owners' hearts Tseng Yi-ju, from Taiwan, works in her pet studio in Xiamen, Fujian province. WANG JINGHAN/FOR CHINA DAILY Tseng Yi-ju, who comes from Taiwan, has served hundreds of pet-owning families on the Chinese mainland, helping people decode the unspoken needs of their animals while healing the hearts of the owners. With the rapid expansion of the pet market and a growing focus on the human-animal emotional bond, she has found a clear direction for her entrepreneurial career in this emerging field in Xiamen, Fujian province. "Xiamen feels just like home to me," Tseng said, noting that her move to the coastal city in 2021 was eased by its familiar climate, warm hospitality and strong government support for Taiwan entrepreneurs — including intellectual property workshops that greatly accelerated her start-up's growth. "People increasingly treat pets as core family members," Tseng said. Her business integrates patented animal communication training and custom pet accessories. Tseng recalled one corporate executive who joined a session to bridge the gap with younger employees as he wanted to organize pet-centric activities to boost team cohesion, and hoped that understanding pets would help him better connect with the younger generation, as many raise pets. "The initial and primary motivation of most clients is simply to forge a deeper, more meaningful connection with their own pets," Tseng said, noting that proper communication also offers critical solutions to severe animal behavioral issues. Tseng shared a case where an indoor cat was constantly biting its own fur bald despite medical tests showing no physical illness. Through a communication session, she discovered the cat felt disturbed and unsafe due to its noisy environment. This was because the cat owner's former apartment had poor soundproofing and creaky floors. The owner later reported that the self-harming behavior stopped after she relocated to a quieter residence. Tseng also helps owners navigate emotional crises during pets' final days. She recalled a client who enrolled because his dog was extremely old, deeply desiring to understand and accompany his companion through its final stage. Another client sought Tseng's help for an aging cat suffering from severe organ failure following major liver surgery. During that emotional session, they spent most of their time addressing the owner's past regrets and saying a proper goodbye. The cat remarkably stabilized afterward, allowing the owner to adjust his life and maximize their remaining time. Liu Jingruo, a Xiamen resident, experienced the deep emotional impact of this practice when she sought Tseng's help for her 17-year-old poodle, Youyou, which suffered from a painful, ruptured abdominal cyst. "Veterinarians across the city warned me that Youyou was too old to survive an operation," Liu said. However, through a joint session with Tseng, she learned that the dog actually desired the surgery so it could leave the world with a whole body. Tseng maintained constant communication with the owner and the dog right up to the operation. Just three hours after surgery, the elderly poodle managed to stand up independently. "I burst into tears when I saw it. It was so tough," Liu said. "Though Youyou later passed away, the experience left me with absolutely no lingering regrets." The experience inspired Liu to study animal communication herself, finding it deeply therapeutic. She now allows her middle-school child to join the training to help the teenager understand the pure, selfless love that animals offer. Liu said that there are times when her child prefers to confide in the family pet rather than speak to her. "The animal might give the child a gentle gaze or a very calming feeling," she said. Sun Xiaonan, another student, found that studying communication heightened her ability to manage multi-pet households, especially after she adopted a fierce stray cat that bullied her resident pet. Sun discovered that her resident cat was enduring immense stress just to keep the peace and spare its owner from conflict. By providing targeted reassurance, Sun successfully gave the animal an emotional outlet, preventing further stress accumulation. "Having reliable, trustworthy animal communicators is essential for modern families," Sun said, adding that she believes this specialized emotional support is quickly shaping up to be a major future trend across the mainland market. Liu Yizhou and Wang Jinghan contributed to this story.

item.title: Fujian league attracts cross-Strait players
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
Fujian league attracts cross-Strait players Team Xiamen and Team Jinmen exchange gifts before a friendly match in Xiamen, Fujian province, on July 5. [Photo provided to CHINA DAILY] Editor's note: The Taiwan question is a key focus for China and the international community. China Daily is publishing a series of reports to track hot Taiwan-related topics and address disinformation from the Democratic Progressive Party administration. The Fujian city soccer league is inviting Taiwan players to compete on the Chinese mainland, and welcoming residents from across the Strait to enjoy the matches firsthand to deepen compatriot affinities and bring hearts closer together. Representing Fujian province's nine cities and the Pingtan Comprehensive Experimental Zone, 10 teams and nearly 500 amateur players are competing in the tournament, which will conclude with the final in October. To boost cross-Strait integration, Fujian — the primary ancestral home for Taiwan compatriots — allows every participating team to add two Taiwan players to its roster. By August, 19 Taiwan players had joined different city teams, according to the Fujian provincial administration of sport. Data show that more than 1,500 people from Taiwan have attended matches across Fujian, and that the league serves as an active catalyst for deepening cross-Strait people-to-people exchanges. Ni Pei-hsu, 24, from Taiwan, joined Fuzhou's soccer club in late June after learning about the recruitment online and was drawn by the massive crowds. It's his first time playing on the mainland.

item.title: DPP criticized for separatist rhetoric amid Malaysia's support for one-China principle
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-26
DPP criticized for separatist rhetoric amid Malaysia's support for one-China principle A Chinese mainland spokeswoman on Wednesday denounced Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities for spreading separatist fallacies and using economic pressure to pursue "Taiwan independence" in response to Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's recent remarks in support of the one-China principle. Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news conference that the Chinese mainland appreciated Malaysia's upholding of the one-China principle. Anwar said in a recent interview with Al Jazeera that he sees Taiwan as part of China. Drawing a parallel with Malaysia, he added that "if one province decides to break up … I will protect the sanctity and unity of the nation." Taiwan's external affairs department later voiced its protest on Aug 18. It claimed that Anwar's remarks "denigrated Taiwan's sovereignty" and warned that Malaysia's support for the one-China principle could "undermine Taiwan businesses' confidence in investing in Malaysia". "There is only one China in the world, and Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory," Zhang said, rejecting the DPP authorities' claims regarding the island's so-called sovereignty. She accused the DPP authorities of stubbornly adhering to a separatist stance, spreading fallacies advocating "Taiwan independence" and repeatedly pressuring relevant countries through trade and investment. Such actions, she said, expose their efforts to pursue "Taiwan independence" through economic and trade pressure.

item.title: Ningbo-Taiwan Hockey Exchange Tournament Concludes in Fenghua, Ningbo, Forging Cross-Strait Friendships Through Sports
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Ningbo-Taiwan Hockey Exchange Tournament Concludes in Fenghua, Ningbo, Forging Cross-Strait Friendships Through Sports Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-25
Aug 25(Taiwan.cn)—On the morning of August 21, the "Tides Rise Across the Strait! Joy at Xuedou Mountain" Ningbo-Taiwan Hockey Exchange Tournament in Fenghua, Ningbo, drew to a rousing close. Nearly 40 athletes from Taiwan and Fenghua competed together, engaging in a cross-Strait sports dialogue with hockey as the medium. The competition venue buzzed with excitement. Players from both sides swung their sticks, passed rapidly, and demonstrated excellent teamwork and competitive spirit amid swift offensive-defensive transitions. "The atmosphere here is fantastic. Players from both sides respect one another and give their all on the pitch. The Fenghua athletes have made remarkable progress," said Mr. Zhuang, a player from the Taiwan team. He noted that hockey has a development history of nearly 50 years in Taiwan, with solid foundations there, while the sport has only gained popularity in Fenghua in recent years. "Still, we can feel their enthusiasm for learning and their rapid improvement. We hope that events like this will enable players from both sides to grow together through competition." "Sports are a vital bond for enhancing affection among cross-Strait compatriots. Going forward, we will continue to build more diverse exchange platforms. Focusing on sports, culture, tourism, talent, and other sectors, we will deepen practical cooperation between Fenghua and Taiwan, so that compatriots across the Strait grow closer through interaction," said an official from the Taiwan Affairs Office of Fenghua District.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Fenghua, Ningbo City) Related Stories

item.title: Tanghe County Hosts Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience for Taiwan Compatriots and Relatives
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-25
Tanghe County Hosts Intangible Cultural Heritage Experience for Taiwan Compatriots and Relatives Source: Taiwan.cnUpdated: 2026-08-25
Aug 25(Taiwan.cn)—To promote China’s fine traditional culture, enrich the cultural lives of local Taiwan compatriots and their relatives, deepen cross-Strait cultural integration, and foster shared identity, the Taiwan Affairs Office of Tanghe County, Nanyang City, hosted a hands-on experience event featuring Song-style brocade round fans on August 19. Using intangible cultural heritage as an emotional bond, the event helped further bridge the psychological distance between compatriots across the Strait. At the venue, staff provided a detailed introduction to the cultural significance of Song brocade and the auspicious meanings associated with round fans. With pre-prepared materials-including brocade fabric, fan ribs, and tassels-they demonstrated the entire production process step by step. Participants received hands-on guidance on fabric bonding, accessory assembly, and fan-surface finishing, while their questions during the process were answered in detail. The Taiwan compatriots and their relatives focused intently on their creations and exchanged ideas with one another. By carefully cutting fabric, applying adhesives, and decorating with tassels, each participant completed their own unique intangible-heritage round fan. Through this immersive experience, attendees gained a firsthand appreciation for the charm of traditional intangible cultural crafts and developed a deeper understanding of the shared cultural roots that unite compatriots across the Strait.(Jointly reported by Taiwan.cn and the Taiwan Affairs Office of Tanghe County, Nanyang City) Related Stories

item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.
